claim: In standard MoE under expert parallelism, the per-layer cost of the two blocking all-to-alls is 2(M-1)*alpha + 2*K*T*D*b/(M*B) under the alpha-beta model, so the bandwidth term scales linearly with tokens per device T and inversely with device count M and per-link bandwidth B.
stance_target: the repo's claim that expert parallelism's all-to-all cost is set by tokens x hidden dim / (devices x link bandwidth) on this fabric
scope_conditions: Single MoE layer distributed over M devices, N/M experts per device, T tokens, hidden dim D, b bytes/element, alpha-beta (Hockney) model; Appendix B.1
quoted_support: Afterwards it produces a token-to-expert index tensor as dispatch assignment used to pack token buffers, which are sent to multiple target devices via blocking All-to-All: tA2A = (M-1) alpha + K * T * D * b / (M * B). ... Total per-layer cost is TMoE = trouting + texpert + 2(M-1) alpha + 2 K * T * D * b / (M * B).

claim: Measured on their own EP testbed, standard MoE prefill throughput drops ~19% going from M=1 (22,346.66 tok/s) to M=2 (18,034.84 tok/s) and does not recover at M=3 (18,558.08) or M=4 (18,355.43) — the blocking all-to-all plus the non-parallelizable router barrier costs roughly a fifth of throughput as soon as a second device is added.
stance_target: the claim that any expert-parallel split of a MoE layer imposes a step cost on this class of fabric
scope_conditions: Model at scale S (92.44M params), prefill T=1,024 tokens in one forward pass, K=3, batch size 1, bf16, mean of 10 reps after 3 warmups; accelerator model and interconnect NOT stated
quoted_support: Standard MoE throughput drops sharply when moving from M=1 to M=2, with Prefill falls by ~19%, and decode falls by ~21%, with little recovery at M=3 or M=4.

claim: Decode throughput under EP falls from 57.90 tok/s at M=1 to 45.65 at M=2, 45.61 at M=3 and 44.67 at M=4 for standard MoE, i.e. the penalty is paid once at the first split rather than growing with device count.
stance_target: whether EP cost scales with device count or is a fixed step at the first split
scope_conditions: Scale S model, decode 128 tokens autoregressively with T=1 per step, K=3, batch 1, bf16

claim: Routing-Free MoE, which replaces the blocking dispatch all-to-all with a non-blocking all-gather plus asynchronous point-to-point combine, retains >=97.8% of single-device prefill throughput and >=95.6% of decode throughput at M=4, and beats standard MoE by 1.19x prefill and 1.12x decode at M=4.
stance_target: the strong form of 'expert parallelism is unusable on a slow fabric' — the cost is in the dispatch barrier and blocking all-to-all, not in having multiple devices at all
scope_conditions: Scale S model, prefill T=1,024 and decode 128 steps, K=Keff=3, batch 1, bf16; hardware unstated
quoted_support: In contrast, Routing-Free MoE retains >=97.8% of its single-device prefill throughput and >=95.6% of its decode throughput at M=4 ... At M=4, Routing-Free MoE delivers 1.19x higher prefill throughput and 1.12x higher decode throughput.

claim: The barrier-synchronization saving of the routing-free design is (M-2)*alpha, strictly positive for all M>=3, while the bandwidth-term difference (K+1-M)*T*D*b/(M*B) only favours it when M < K+1 — so the advantage is structural at M>=3 and bandwidth-dependent otherwise.
stance_target: the conditions under which an EP variant can beat standard MoE on a bandwidth-starved fabric
scope_conditions: Same alpha-beta model; prefill regime (large T) vs decode regime (T=1)
quoted_support: For communication, the barrier synchronization saving delta-alpha = (M-2) alpha is strictly positive for all M >= 3, independent of input size or activation ratio. The bandwidth terms differ as delta-B = (K + 1 - M) * T * D * b / (M * B), which favors Routing-Free MoE when M < K + 1.

claim: The paper validates MoE architectures at three scales up to 0.8B parameters, with the smallest scale S at 92.44M parameters, each trained from scratch for one epoch on OpenWebText — establishing that a 0.1-0.8B MoE training campaign is a normal research unit, not a toy.
stance_target: the feasibility of MoE experiments in the 0.1B-1B range on a single 5-GPU box
scope_conditions: Mixtral-style HuggingFace implementation (GQA, RoPE, SwiGLU, RMSNorm); OpenWebText, one epoch; scales S/M/L
quoted_support: We validate Routing-Free MoE across three scales up to 0.8B with extensive experiments ... Each model is trained on OpenWebText (Gokaslan et al., 2019) from scratch for one epoch.

claim: Routing-Free MoE outperforms standard MoE, AoE and ReMoE at every scale on validation perplexity and downstream average (+0.80pp mean), and stays stable where standard MoE diverges at learning rate 2e-3 — evidence that routing design, not just scale, drives small-MoE trainability.
stance_target: the repo's plan to run MoE experiments at ~1B scale on this box
scope_conditions: Iso-FLOP comparison (FLOPs matched within ~1%), OpenWebText one epoch, scales S/M/L up to 0.8B
quoted_support: This is evident at scale S, where MoE fails at alpha = 2e-3 while Routing-Free MoE remains stable throughout training. ... Table 7 reports per-scale statistics. The mean improvement is positive at every scale (+0.80 pp ...).

claim: The EP measurements are inference-stage only (prefill and decode), on an accelerator and interconnect the paper never names, so the 19-21% M=1->M=2 penalty cannot be read as a measurement on a Gen2 x4 no-P2P fabric — it is a lower bound for such a fabric.
stance_target: how far the paper's EP numbers can be transferred to the CMP 170HX box
scope_conditions: Appendix B.1-B.2; no GPU model, node count or link type stated anywhere in the paper
quoted_support: All runs use batch size 1 with input tokens sampled randomly from OpenWebText, bfloat16 precision, and report the mean over 10 repetitions after 3 warmup ones.
